info.title: MailHQ API
info.description:
## Domain onboarding guide

Send and receive mail with your own domain. The domain can stay at its current registrar. An admin requests onboarding and verifies domain ownership; once DNS is configured with the records shown in the admin, you can use your own email addresses.

[Start domain onboarding](/settings#domain-connection) · [Admin](/settings) · [Webmail](/webmail)

### 01 · Request onboarding

Prepare a domain whose DNS you control. In **Settings → External domain onboarding**, an admin selects a Stalwart mail service subscription, enters the domain (for example `example.com`) and clicks **Generate verification record**.

Only admins can request, verify and view onboarding settings. Domains and mailboxes are currently managed centrally by admins; domain owners never need to hand over registrar accounts or DNS keys to this service.

Admin tip: once provisioned, the domain joins the existing mailbox management and redemption rules. Generic redemption codes or products without a domain restriction will include the new domain; before hosting an external domain, review and restrict the allowed domains.

### 02 · Add a TXT record to verify ownership

1. In the admin, open the domain's onboarding details and copy the name and value of the **Domain ownership** TXT record.
2. At the DNS provider the domain currently uses, add that TXT record. Whether the host field needs the full domain depends on your provider; avoid appending the domain suffix twice.
3. Wait for DNS to propagate, then click **Verify ownership and connect** in the admin. Once verified, the domain is provisioned on the mail server and added to the managed list.

Pending verification records are valid for 7 days; after that, click **Refresh verification record**, update the value in DNS and verify again. Ownership of an already provisioned domain does not expire because of this. You can keep the verification TXT for auditing; removing it does not disable a provisioned domain. No MX change is needed at this stage, so existing mailboxes keep receiving mail.

If the page shows **Confirming provisioning**, use **Check again** to read the result; if it shows **Needs manual review**, an admin should check the domain on the server first to avoid creating it twice.

### 03 · Prepare mailboxes, then migrate mail

Provisioning status and mail DNS checks are shown separately. Once ownership verification and server provisioning are done, you can create mailboxes on the domain, such as `you@example.com`, without switching mail routing first.

If the domain already has mailboxes, create the matching accounts and confirm passwords and forwarding rules before migrating any old mail you want to keep. Creating a mailbox does not copy historical mail from the old provider.

Move on only once the new mailboxes are ready. For a while after switching MX, some senders may still use the old records, so keep the old service and check mail on both sides.

### 04 · Configure mail DNS from the admin, switch MX last

In **Settings → Domains**, click the domain's **DNS settings / check**, or open its details from the onboarding request list. The admin shows the exact names, values, MX priorities and check results this domain needs. Use those records; the table below explains what each kind is for.

| Record | Purpose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MX | Delivers new mail to this service | Use the target and priority shown in the admin; switch it last, once mailboxes and migration are ready. |
| TXT · SPF | Authorizes servers to send for the domain | A domain can have only one SPF record. If one exists, merge the authorizations and keep other sending services still in use. |
| TXT · DKIM | Verifies mail signatures | Copy each selector and public key exactly as shown in the admin. Do not use signing records from other domains or servers. |
| TXT · DMARC | Declares the mail authentication policy | Optional and recommended; start with `p=none`. If a policy exists, review it first and do not overwrite existing quarantine or reject policies. |

Set mail-related records to **DNS only**; do not enable web proxying. Unless an admin says otherwise, there is no need to create `mail.your-domain` or get a certificate for it; mail clients use the server name shown in the admin.

Before switching MX, review the domain settings at the old provider. Some providers may still deliver mail sent within their own platform to their old mailboxes, so the old provider's delivery mode may also need adjusting.

### 05 · Check again and start using it

After saving DNS, click **Check again** in the domain details. The page shows the records currently found and why any are missing, conflicting or failed to resolve. DNS caches take time to update; if records don't match yet, confirm the names and values, then wait for the old records' caches to expire.

| Item | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| Incoming mail | IMAP · 993 · SSL/TLS |
| Outgoing mail | SMTP · 465 · SSL/TLS |
| Server | The server name shown on the admin page |
| Sign-in | Full email address + mailbox password |

Use [Webmail](/webmail) or your own mail client. Whether webmail is available depends on the domain being provisioned and the settings an admin has enabled.

Test receiving and sending separately from an independent external mailbox, and check the spam folder. Passing DNS checks and SPF / DKIM / DMARC does not guarantee delivery to the inbox at Gmail or other services.

The live settings on the admin page are authoritative for each domain's records. [Manage domain onboarding](/settings#domain-connection).

## API access

### Creating keys and authenticating

First generate an API key in [Settings → API keys](/settings/api-keys), choosing the permissions and expiry you need (it can be set to never expire), then enter the full key under Authorize.

All `/api/v1` endpoints accept only `Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>`. A browser sign-in cookie cannot replace a Bearer key, and each operation also requires the matching scope. Granting only a write scope does not grant read access. After a key is revoked, further requests with it are rejected.

### Scope

This API manages the Stalwart mail service connected to MailHQ.

It currently covers the server list, domain verification and provisioning, importing existing domains, enabling/disabling domains, mailboxes, passwords, status, storage quota, daily sending limits, notes, regular aliases, distribution lists, forwarding, a per-domain catch-all, alias domains and domain connection details, with batch operations. It does not offer reading/searching/deleting mail content, sending mail, autoresponders, spam policies or reseller management.

Below, each operation's scope, parameters, responses and examples are listed by group. The API base URL is `/api/v1` on this site.

### Regular aliases and domain management

Regular aliases use the `aliases:read` / `aliases:write` scopes. The target must be an existing managed user mailbox on the same domain; aliases can be created, renamed, enabled/disabled, re-described and deleted, but the target mailbox cannot be changed. Special or read-only aliases must be managed in Stalwart. Aliases are neither external forwarding nor catch-all.

`GET /domains/{id}/catch-all` reads and `PUT /domains/{id}/catch-all` sets the mailbox that receives mail for addresses of the domain nobody holds: `{ "destination": "postmaster@example.com" }` (an existing managed mailbox of the same domain), or `{ "destination": null }` to reject such mail, the default. A catch-all accepts every guessed or mistyped address, so it attracts spam.

`PUT /domains/{id}/status` accepts `{ "enabled": true }` or `false` and enables or disables the domain on Stalwart. `DELETE /domains/{id}` still only removes the local record and cannot delete the remote domain. Writes to domains and aliases require the admin role and the matching write scope.

### Alias domains

An alias domain is an additional domain name whose addresses deliver to the mailboxes of a primary domain: mail for `user@alias.example` goes to the mailbox of `user@primary.example`, and the primary domain's aliases, lists and catch-all apply too. `POST /domains/{id}/domain-aliases` with `{ "domain": "alias.example" }` records the request and returns the ownership TXT record; after publishing it, `POST /domains/{id}/domain-aliases/{aliasId}/verify` adds the name on the mail server, and `GET` on the alias lists the MX record it needs to receive mail. An alias domain is for receiving: mail sent from its addresses is signed with the primary domain's DKIM key. Onboard a domain of its own when it has to send under its own name.

### Distribution lists

Distribution lists use the `lists:read` / `lists:write` scopes. A list is an address of a domain that delivers a copy of every message to all of its members; it has no mailbox, cannot sign in and does not count towards the workspace's mailbox limit. `GET /lists?domainId=…` lists a domain's lists with their members, `POST /lists` creates one, and `PATCH /lists/{listId}` renames it, changes its description and adds or removes members. Members that are not mailboxes managed by the workspace are refused unless the request sets `allowExternal: true`: the mail server then forwards everything sent to the list, spam included, to those outside addresses. The list's address must be free among mailboxes (pending and deleted ones included), aliases, forwarding addresses and other lists.

### Legal holds

Legal holds use the `holds:read` / `holds:write` scopes (admin keys only). `POST /holds` places a hold on one mailbox (`mailboxId`) or on every mailbox of a domain (`domain`) with a `name`, a `reason` and an optional `endsAt`; `POST /holds/{id}/release` releases it with a `reason`. While a hold is active the mailbox cannot be deleted permanently or purged from the recycle bin (`409 legal_hold`); deleting it into the recycle bin still works. A hold preserves the mailbox, not individual messages: the mailbox's user can still delete their own mail, and this is not a certified archive.

### Reports

`GET /reports/inactive-mailboxes`, `GET /reports/storage` and `GET /reports/top-senders` are read-only reports under `mailboxes:read`: mailboxes with no WebMail sign-in and no mail for 30, 60 or 90 days, mailbox usage per domain from daily samples, and today's top senders by daily sending-limit usage. They are computed from records MailHQ keeps, not from the mail server's own counters: sign-ins and sends of mail apps over IMAP / SMTP are not seen.

### Batch requests and verifying results

`POST /batch` accepts `{ "operations": [...] }` with 1–25 operations and a body of at most 16 KiB, and requires an `Idempotency-Key` of 8–128 letters, digits, hyphens or underscores. Each operation has a unique `id`, an `operation` and an `input`. The whole request's format, base fields and required scopes are validated before the first write, then operations run in order; resource existence, domain ownership and remote state are checked as each one runs.

Returns 200 when everything succeeds and 207 when any operation failed, is uncertain or was not executed. Each `outcome` is `succeeded`, `failed`, `uncertain` or `skipped`. Execution continues after ordinary failures and stops when a result is unclear; completed operations are not rolled back or retried automatically, and responses never include passwords.

The same API key, idempotency key and normalized operations replay the saved result; different content returns 409. After a timeout, first query `GET /batch/{requestId}` with the original key: it returns only the `running` / `completed` / `uncertain` state and timestamps, not the operations or results. `running` and `uncertain` never expire or re-run automatically. Even when it reports `completed`, still check every outcome in the original batch result; it does not mean every operation succeeded.

### Interactive requests and documentation security

All examples use fictional data. The documentation never reads instance configuration, connected domains, mailbox passwords or API keys.

Interactive requests go directly from your browser to this site, without a public request proxy. Keys are not kept after a page refresh; do not enter API keys on shared devices, and never put keys in URLs, code repositories or logs.

tags.description: Provision a domain after verifying ownership, or look up / cancel pending requests.

tags.name: Domains
tags.description: Import existing Stalwart domains and manage local records.

tags.name: Mailboxes
tags.description: Manage mailboxes; passwords and redemption-code links are never returned.

tags.name: Forwarders
tags.description: Forwarding rules between single regular email addresses.

tags.name: Aliases
tags.description: Regular aliases delivering to managed mailboxes on the same domain.

tags.name: Lists
tags.description: Distribution lists: an address of a domain that delivers to all of its members.

tags.name: Legal holds
tags.description: Legal holds: a held mailbox cannot be deleted permanently or purged. A hold preserves the mailbox, not individual messages.

tags.name: Reports
tags.description: Usage reports: inactive mailboxes, storage per domain, top senders. Computed from this app's own records.

tags.name: Batch
tags.description: Manage domains, mailboxes and aliases in ordered batches with persisted idempotent results.

tags.name: Agent tasks
tags.description: An agent follows up email as a given mailbox: it starts from a prompt, sends fully autonomously by default, and continues when replies arrive.

tags.name: Webhooks
tags.description: Signed event webhooks: mailbox, domain, order, bulk job and security events POSTed to your https address, with retries and a delivery log.

tags.name: Trace
tags.description: Message trace: the delivery timeline of messages sent or received by the workspace's domains, read from the mail server's logs and queue. Every call is recorded in the activity log.

tags.name: Suppressions
tags.description: The workspace's suppression list: recipients that hard-bounced repeatedly or were added by hand. Advisory: nothing is refused at submission; check an address before sending to it.

get.description:
Requires `trace:read` scope.

What happened to a message: when it was accepted and queued, every delivery attempt with the remote host and its SMTP answer, and whether it ended delivered, deferred (with the next retry) or bounced. At least one of `sender`, `recipient`, `messageId` and `queueId` is required (400 `missing_criteria`); all given criteria must match.

The data comes from the mail server's file logs (Stalwart's own per-message history is Enterprise-only), so only messages still in the logs are found, and steps such as TLS are present only when the server logs them; `tls` and `dkimSigned` are `null` when the log does not say. `queued` lists matching messages still waiting in the outbound queue, read from the queue itself. Each call reads a bounded part of the logs and returns at most 10 messages; while `cursor` is not null, call again with it for older ones. `servers[].exhausted` says nothing more of the workspace's messages was found on that server.

**Off until the platform operator turns it on**: while the platform setting "Workspace admins can use message trace" is off (the default), only a platform admin's key of the default workspace may call this; every other key gets `403 forbidden`, also with the `trace:read` scope.

A key sees only messages whose envelope sender or a recipient is in one of its workspace's domains, and of a message from outside only the recipients in those domains. Nothing else in the answer comes from other workspaces' mail either: `searchedBack`, `servers[].oldest`, `servers[].exhausted` and `cursor` are worked out from the key's own messages, so a search that only other workspaces' mail matches answers exactly like one that nothing matches. To page reliably through mail from a sender who also writes to other workspaces, add one of the workspace's own addresses or domains as `recipient`. **Every call is recorded in the activity log** with the key's id and the search terms, because a trace reveals who wrote to whom. 409 `trace_unavailable`: none of the workspace's domains is bound to a mail server whose management API is configured.
